name: High Seas
subject: Ships, sailing and the sea
tagline: Eleven questions on ships, shipwrecks, pirates and the people who crossed the oceans. Starts easy, ends hard.

questions.q: On which night did the Titanic sink after hitting an iceberg?
questions.w: The night of 14 to 15 April 1912, four days into her maiden voyage from Southampton to New York. About 1,500 of the 2,200 people aboard died.
questions.more: She carried lifeboats for only about half of them, which was legal at the time, and several left half empty. The wreck was found in 1985 by Robert Ballard, two and a half miles down, during a secret US Navy mission to inspect two sunken submarines. Lusitania was torpedoed on 7 May 1915.

questions.q: On a ship, which side is 'port'?
questions.w: The left. Starboard is the right, from the 'steer board', the steering oar old ships carried on that side.
questions.more: Because the steering oar was on the right, ships docked with their left side to the quay, the 'port' side; the older word was 'larboard', dropped because it sounded too much like starboard in a gale. Port has four letters, like left. Navigation lights follow suit: red to port, green to starboard.

questions.q: What is the name of the pirate flag with a white skull and crossed bones on black?
questions.w: The Jolly Roger, flown in the early 1700s to persuade merchant ships to surrender without a fight.
questions.more: Real pirates used many designs: Blackbeard's showed a horned skeleton spearing a heart. The name may come from 'joli rouge', a red flag meaning no quarter. The Golden Age of piracy lasted barely a decade, from about 1715 to 1726, before navies hanged most of its stars.

questions.q: Which explorer's ships completed the first voyage around the world in 1522, though he died in the Philippines before the end?
questions.w: Ferdinand Magellan. Of five ships and about 270 men that left Spain in 1519, one ship and eighteen men came home three years later under Juan Sebastián Elcano.
questions.more: Magellan was Portuguese but sailed for Spain after his own king refused him. The survivors found their careful log was a day out: they had crossed what we now call the date line without knowing it existed. Drake was the first captain to make it all the way round himself, in 1580.

questions.q: What does SOS, the Morse code distress signal, stand for?
o: Nothing; it was chosen because it is easy to send and recognise
questions.w: Nothing at all. Three dots, three dashes, three dots was adopted internationally in 1908 simply because it is unmistakable; the phrases came afterwards.
questions.more: The Titanic's operators sent both the old signal CQD and the new SOS. Voice radio later adopted 'Mayday', from the French 'm'aidez', help me, coined by a London airport radio officer in 1923 because most traffic was to Paris. SOS is also a palindrome and reads the same upside down, which helps when stamped in sand or snow.

questions.q: Which canal, opened in 1914, lets ships pass between the Atlantic and the Pacific without rounding South America?
questions.w: The Panama Canal, 82 kilometres long, which lifts ships 26 metres through locks into a man-made lake and down the other side.
questions.more: A French attempt led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, builder of Suez, collapsed in the 1880s after some 22,000 workers died, mostly of yellow fever and malaria. The United States finished it after backing Panama's secession from Colombia, and handed it over in 1999. Because of the isthmus's shape, a ship going from the Atlantic to the Pacific actually travels south-east.

questions.q: In 1789 the crew of which Royal Navy ship mutinied in the Pacific and set Captain Bligh adrift in an open boat?
questions.w: HMS Bounty, which had spent five idle months in Tahiti collecting breadfruit plants for the Caribbean plantations.
questions.more: Bligh and eighteen loyal men then sailed 6,700 kilometres to Timor in a seven-metre launch, one of the great feats of navigation. The mutineers under Fletcher Christian hid on Pitcairn Island, where their descendants still live. HMS Beagle carried Darwin, and Endeavour was Cook's ship.

questions.q: What is the bulbous bow, the rounded protrusion below the waterline at the front of most big ships, for?
o: Reducing drag by cancelling out the bow wave
questions.w: Cutting fuel use: it creates its own wave that partly cancels the ship's bow wave, reducing drag by up to 15 per cent at cruising speed.
questions.more: The idea was noticed on battleships with ram bows around 1900 and worked out properly by Japanese naval architects in the 1960s. It only helps at the speed and load it was designed for; container ships slowed down after 2008 to save fuel, and many had their bulbs cut off and replaced with shorter ones.

questions.q: Which trophy, first contested off the Isle of Wight in 1851, is the oldest international sporting trophy still competed for?
questions.w: The America's Cup, named after the schooner America that beat the British fleet. Queen Victoria asked who was second and was told 'Your Majesty, there is no second'.
questions.more: The New York Yacht Club then held it for 132 years, the longest winning streak in sport, until Australia II and its secret winged keel won in 1983. Modern Cup boats are foiling catamarans and monohulls that fly above the water at over 50 knots. New Zealand defended it in 2024 in Barcelona.

questions.q: The problem of finding a ship's longitude at sea was finally solved in the 1700s by a self-taught English carpenter who built what?
o: An accurate marine clock, the chronometer
questions.w: A chronometer. John Harrison's H4, a large pocket watch finished in 1759, lost only five seconds on a voyage to Jamaica, which translates to about a mile of error.
questions.more: Parliament had offered 20,000 pounds in 1714 after a fleet ran aground on the Scilly Isles with the loss of 2,000 men. Local time from the sun compared with Greenwich time on the clock gives longitude, four minutes per degree. The astronomers on the prize board fought Harrison for years, and he got the full reward only at 80, after the king intervened.

questions.q: Which of these ships were sunk by enemy action, rather than by accident or weather? Select all that apply.
questions.w: Lusitania was torpedoed by a U-boat in 1915, Bismarck was hunted down by the Royal Navy in 1941, and USS Arizona was bombed at Pearl Harbor. Titanic hit an iceberg and the liner Andrea Doria sank after a collision in fog in 1956.
questions.more: The Lusitania sinking, with 128 Americans among the 1,200 dead, helped turn US opinion towards war. Bismarck sank the pride of the Royal Navy, HMS Hood, three days before she was caught; only three of Hood's 1,418 crew survived. Arizona still lies at Pearl Harbor with most of her 1,177 dead aboard, leaking a few drops of oil a day.
